the Chinese very largely from the individuals with whom we may come in contact in this country. It is generally known that these as a rule belong to the lower classes, and that they do not fairly represent the whole of the people over there. We have to deal in these days, not merely with the individuals who come to us in this country, our laundry-men, our vegetable men, or our keepers of restaurants, or our tailors; but we have sooner or later to deal with the whole of the great people of China. We must remember that China represents a very ancient and a very high type of civilization. It is quite true that for a good many centuries Chinese civilization rejnained almost stationary, but one reason for that was that the Chinese shut themselves off from contact with the larger world outside, a policy which some in this countiy would like us to adopt with regard at least to the oriental races. We in the west have been superior very laregly because of the industrial revolution with all that it has brought to us in the advancement of science, and in the possibility of large-scale production, and may I add also in +he possibility of our securing arms which from the military standpoint have made us dominant throughout the world. But now, as thoughtful students have observed, we are losing that advantage which we have had for the last hundred years or more, and the Orient is beginning to open its dobrs to western science, to western civilization, to western industry, and to western militarism. When the hundreds of millions of people across the ocean have gained possession of the tools of production and destruction, we have no advantage, or comparatively little advantage over them. There is not much wonder that some writers are afraid of this "rising tide of colour". It is a real danger; yet there are other ways of meeting it than by attempting to turn back the rising tide. It is a dangerous proceeding for a comparatively small portion of the human race to attempt by physical force to beat back the great masses of the coloured and darker people of the world. Very great changes have come within recent years in the Orient. With regard to China, Professor A. E. Ross, Professor John Dewey, Hon. Bertrand Russell, and a host of other writers, have been telling us of the changes that are taking place in their eastern civilization. They impress upon us there is a great intellectual awakening- an awakening that may be faintly understood, if we could realize the changes that took place in Europe at the time of the renaissance. The people are being given the literature of

China in their own spoken language, and there is being translated into Chinese the literature of western Europe. A wonderful intellectual activity is consequently taking place among the masses all over China. Many of us, of course, are compelled to get at second hand these accounts of what the Chinese are doing. A gentleman returning a short time ago from China made the astounding statement that in his judgment Peking was destined to be the intellectual centre of the world. I can hardly accept that, but I cannot reject the testimony of men who are recognized authorities throughout Europe, and who declare that wonderful changes are taking place. It is a well-known fact that when an ancient civilization is touched and fertilized by a newer and different type of civilization the results are sometimes remarkable.
In view of the fact that the world has become so unified industrially and commercially, and in its political relationships, it would seem as if we had arrived at that juncture where we should very definitely attempt to establish a better understanding among the great peoples of the earth. I was very much interested in a resolution, to which reference was made on the floor of the House some few weeks ago, which was forwarded by the Federation of Canadian Students, urging that scholarships be established by the-government of Canada which would bring considerable numbers of the representatives of various nations to this country, and on the other hand would send out Canadian students to those countries for the purpose of studying conditions there. If this suggestion could be carried out it would be a very definite contribution on our part towards establishing better world relationships. In opposition to the view expressed the other day, that as far as possible we should try to keep out students I would urge on the contrary, that we should heartily welcome them. If we have anything superior in our civilization to give them, by all means let them come over and discover it, so that they may learn what has made our nation great and may take that knowledge back to their country with them. We must get away from the old idea that we would lose by their gain, that we are superior so long as we can keep knowledge and information and science to ourselves and keep these other people more or less in ignorance. I would say rather that we should welcome their students. Let us take them in and give them the very best we have to offer intellectually and morally. On the other hand, I

Chinese Immigration
should like to think that China has something worth while to offer to us. For years she was in advance of us intellectually, and led the way in some of the industrial discoveries by which the world has been blessed. She may still have something to contribute to the progress of the world intellectually and spiritually. I am looking, however, to the practical side of the matter. If we are to avoid frictions in the future there must be a better mutual understanding among the various peoples of the world. Personally, I believe that the chief cause of modern wars is economic, but I do not believe it is the exclusive cause. One of the dangers to-day lies in the fact that we do not understand one another's position, that as nations we are prejudiced one against the other. In this discussion we have heard a good deal about exclusion. While I am not opposed to a certain measure of precaution in this direction, feeling as I do that we have a right to protect the standards of this young country, at the same time I cannot let this opportunity pass without pleading with the government and the House that they treat this question in a broad way. Do not let our prejudice blind us to the greatness of the question or to the possibilities that are open to us, as a people, of making our contribution to the solution of the great world problems which are pressing upon us in these days as never before.

If I may be permitted, I should like to point out a mistake in this section. Unless I am utterly unable to interpret it, the section as it is printed is most emphatically wrong. In subsection 1 of paragraph (c) there appears the word "merchants," with whatever amendments may now have been passed. The next paragraph refers to students, and it goes on to say, "who shall substantiate their status." The substantiation called for refers only to the students and not to the merchants, as the section is at present worded; whereas I have no doubt it is the intention of the government to require this substantiation of status on the part of both merchants and students. Paragraph (2) reads:
Students coming to Canada for the purpose of attendance, and while in actual attendance, at any Canadian university or college authorized by statute or charter to confer degrees, who shall substantiate their status to the satisfaction of the controller, etc.
Clearly the merchant does not come under that provision; the relative "who" obviously refers to the students. Is there no legal gentleman on the opposite side who can take up this point? If there is not I shall have to solicit the assistance of the leader of the Opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Objection was taken by my hon. friend to the clause as drafted, and he suggested that we add the words "peace officer," so that any officer might take into custody a Chinaman who was illegally in the country. That has been done by the amendment to 26. I beg to move this amendment, which is as follows:
26. Whenever any officer or peace officer has reason to believe that any person of Chinese origin or descent has entered or remains in Canada contrary to the provisions of this act or of the Chinese Immigration Act, chapter ninety-five of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, or any amendment thereof, he may, without a warrant apprehend such person, and if such person is unable to prove to the satisfaction of the officer that he has been properly admitted into and is legally entitled to remain in Canada, the officer may detain such person in custody and bring him before the nearest controller for examination, and if the controller finds that he has entered or remains in Canada contrary to the provisions of this act or of the Chinese Immigration Act or any amendment thereof, such person shall be deported to the country of his birth or citizenship, subject to the same right of appeal as is provided in the case of a person applying for original entry to Canada. Where any person is examined under this section the burden of proof of Such person's right to be or remain in Canada shall rest upon him. Where an order for deportation is made under this section and in the circumstances of the case the expenses of deportation cannot be charged to the transportation company, such expenses shall be paid by the person being deported if able to pay, and, if not, by His Majesty.

What we were providing was that we would only pay for the standard of road to which this department agreed.
Can the minister tell us what the change was? It must have been tremendously expensive to jump from $34,000 to $72,000.

I am not sure that I am not getting beyond my depth in discussing this matter. They changed the standard and put on a great deal better surface than the standard to which we had agreed. I would not like to say offhand what they did. That is outside of our purview. The province did that in addition to anything we expended.
Supply-State
Was the department asked to contribute on the basis of $72,000?
I would imagine the federal department would be asked to contribute anything any province would hope to be able to get. There is no doubt in my mind that they asked for it but did not get it.

If the minister feels sure about that, I do not want to press it unduly, but I want to know for certain whether they did ask for the contribution from this government on the basis of $72,000 a mile. '
No doubt about that at all.
The minister said there was an agreement, between the Dominion and the province.
Yes, all these roads were built under agreement.
In writing and signed?
Yes, I will give the hon. member a copy of it any time.
I would like to have that. Is there a fair wage clause in it?

We do not construct. The province would construct. I imagine they would pay the rate of wages demanded in that locality. These details are for the province. It is one of the cases where the Dominion hands over its money under certain restrictions as to expense, but the province expends the money. I do not know anything about the details. It is a public road. A copy of any agreement as to roadmaking is at the disposal of the House or any member of it.
I can assure the minister that we require considerably more information, and it will take more than a few minutes. But we are quite willing to go on.
I cannot be here after six o'clock. I was hopeful of putting it through.
With reference to the continuation of the Brantford-Hamiiton highway across the county I represent, I certainly would like to get some information.

If my hon. friend would let me- know what he wants, I would be glad to get it for him. It would take a cart to bring over all the documents in the department in regard to this matter.

(ii)	Securities in possession of the Custodian. Under the provisions of paragraph 10 of the Annex
to section 4, part X, of the Treaty of Versailles, Germany was obligated to transfer to Canada all certificates for shares, bonds, debentures, securities, etc. To date there has been received from Germany in this connection 38,858 shares of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and $148,580.00 Note Certificates of the same company. I understood the minister to make a statement about property sequestrated in Germany, was that correct?

Supply-State-War Claims
That was Canadian property in Germany taken over by the German government.
What sort of property would it be?

They were claims by Canadian merchants. For example there was a claim by one of our large manufacturing companies which was adjusted a long time ago. Most of what the minister has been telling us is history. Take for example his account of what transpired in Germany. That happened long ago.

Certainly.
Sir HENRY" DRAYTON-: He has been settling these claims and getting back the money. For example there was the claim of the Massey Harris Company. A lot of this settling was done a long time ago. The adjusting of these matters was supposed to have been settled long since. Mr. Mulvey was sent over in order to wind it up.
Not wind it up.

Well, to arrange a system of settlement that would properly function; to get rid of all this expenditure and try and secure some final action on these matters. In spite of that I observe the vote is continuing just the same. What we are trying to find out is, what was done last year and not what has been done since the war. All these Canadian Pacific Railway shares were in long ago.
No, not all, we are getting them almost daily.
How many did you get in this year?

I could not tell my hon. friend exactly how many shares. I know we have not got them all in; they are coming in weekly and monthly; I could not say daily; and we are dealing with them just as they have been dealt with in the past.

The principal
thing done this year was to issue claims for some $62,918.76 on behalf of Canadian debtors.
My hon. friend should not say that.

Well, what else
was there?

What I have read to my hon. friend related to the work of the clearing office. It has been going on just the same during the past year as in the year before. We have the same officials and the same 159J
work is going on. We have to carry on a correspondence between the clearing offices and attend to other business. I have asked my officials if there is any possibility of getting along with a fewer number of employees and a smaller expenditure and from the statements made to me I do not see how we can.

What is the
attitude of the minister in regard to it? This work is going on apparently the same as it has in the past although there is not the same necessity for it. What is the idea? Is this to be a perpetual department?

Claims are still coming in from Germany and they have to be considered now just the same as they have been in the past. Possibly there are not as large amounts of money involved, the claims now, possibly, are smaller but we are trying to get then! cleared up and we need the staff to do the work.

My recollection was that a time limit was fixed for all this sort of business and it should be up by now;
I do not know whether it has been extended. What I want to know is whether this is to be a perpetual office or not. I simply want to get the facts?

I cannot tell my hon. friend just how long the work will be going on. He knows very well that you cannot settle up such matters as these in a week, or a month, or even a year. I am sure the staff have been working as faithfully as they could and with all possible speed to try and get this matter settled up. We hope to get it settled some time but I cannot say just when.

From what the minister says it is a pretty hopeless looking situation. He says the staff are working hard. Perhaps they are, as to that I cannot say. What I am trying to find out from the minister is when this work will be over. The German claims against Canada numbered 8,643. They have been looked after and all that is left on hand out of all the mess is 475 claims. There is not such an awful lot left to be done as far as that is concerned.
Claims are coming in all the time; they are coming in yet.

How many
claims were received last month? Let us get some idea.

I do not think I can tell my hon. friend that.

Is there no time limit for the filing of claims, or will they be received for all time?
The time has been extended.

How much
longer are you going to go on extending the time?

That is a matter which would be decided by conference between the different clearing offices, but they have not been able to get together recently on account of the difficulty between Germany and France. The whole matter is being worked out by the clearing offices of the different countries interested. This is only a local clearing office here and we have to work through the central clearing office in London. The. time limit has been extended from time to time, and I suppose will continue to be extended until such time as the Powers can get together and come to some conclusion as to the final disposition of the matter.
Who is in charge of this work for the minister's department?
My deputy is the deputy custodian in charge of this work.
What official title has Mr. Pugsley in connection with it?
He is a commissioner under the Inquiries Act to carry on an investigation in connection with the reparations question. He is not identified with my office at all.
Is he steadily employed?
Just as a commissioner to make inquiries on the reparations question under the Inquiries Act.
Is he paid out of this vote?
Paid out of this vote.
How much is it proposed to pay him?
At the rate of $9,000 per year.
Who was his predecessor in this work?
Sir Douglas Hazen, of St. John, was first appointed but later on he expressed a desire to be relieved of this work and Dr. Pugsley was appointed.
How much was paid to Sir Douglas Hazen during the time he acted?
He did not occupy the office. He came up and looked into the matter and decided he would not take it [Mr. CoppJ
Did he not go to Washington? Did he not make some investigation?
I think not.

It is rather strange that the amount supposed to be paid to the Hon. William Pugsley, synchronizes with the salary of the position which he has just given up as lieutenant governor of New Brunswick? It looks to me as if this place had been made for him. I should like to point out to the minister that as long as I can remember that gentleman has never been off the payroll of the government, and I question very much the advisability of appointing him at the salary to which the minister has referred. I doubt very much if it is worth that much to the country. Has it been decided that the claims of private individuals shall have priority over the claims of the Crown in connection with the German moneys in the hands of the custodian?

I cannot quite understand
what you mean?

We are entitled to some reparation from Germany under the terms of the Peace treaty. I understand there are certain German properties in the hands of the custodian. So far none of these reparations have been received by Canada to reimburse her for expenses in connection with the war, and it is not probable, so far as we can see from the turn of events, that we will ever get anything out of Germany. Is it not supposed that the country should be re-imbursed with some of these moneys for part of the expense Canada was put to in connection with the war, and will the claims of the country have priority over the claims of private individuals?

I do not think they will. The investigation is being carried on at the present time because, under the treaty of Peace, the question of reparations and the filing of claims for reparation from Germany was advertised, and a very large number of claims have been filed, I think, amounting to twenty-five or thirty million dollars. Those have been on file in the office for the last two or three years. Some were filed as far back as 1918, Those are being inquired into now, to ascertain whether they are valid claims to be considered and whether the claims are too large. Every one who wishes to file a claim will have an opportunity of appearing before the commissioner himself, or by solicitor or counsel, and placing the facts before the commissioner, and on those facts

the commissioner will make a report to the government. When that is done the question of payment of those claims will have to be decided later on, as a question of policy.
I am not in position to tell my hon. friend or the House or the country, what the final result will be when these claims have been adjudicated upon. We will have a certain amount of money obtained from property we have sold, and shares, stocks, and bonds that we are holding at the present time as custodian or trustee. After the'payment
9 p.m. of the debts between the two countries is arranged there will be a large amount. It is only an estimate but we hope there will be ten, twelve or fourteen million dollars in the hands of the custodian. The question of what will be done with that money, whether it will be applied in satisfaction, or in partial satisfaction, of claims for reparation, is a question of policy to be decided later on. I am not prepared to say how it will be settled. The same is true of the Old Country and the United States. They are carrying on investigations in the United States into the same question, to get information and obtain evidence upon which they can make a report and take action when the time comes to bring the matter to a finality.
Is that question of policy one that will be decided by the federal government or the Imperial government?
I would not like to say what will be done. I think it *null be decided by a-conference between the governments.
When was the commissioner appointed?
On the 13th March last.
Who previously did this work?

No work was being done in regard to it. This commissioner is holding an investigation as to the validity of the claims that have been filed. The claims have been all filed, and he is acting in the position of a judge to hear the claims, take evidence, and make a report as to what claims are valid and what claims are not.
Is there any good reason why this should not be done by a judge of the Exchequer Court? Would he not be the proper person?
Just now they are rather short of judges in the Exchequer Court.
You might make an appointment. *
The Montreal Star says the government is going to appoint an hon. member to the Exchequer Court judgeship.

I am sure any hon. member will agree that the gentleman who has been selected to carry on that work is very well qualified for the position and is a man of splendid legal attainments. He occupied a seat in this parliament for many years, and I have always regarded him as one of the greatest legal minds in the Dominion. I think the hon. member for York-Simbury (Mr. Hanson) and the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter) will agree with me.
Do not slobber over him too much.

I entirely concur in the remarks of the Secretary of State with reference to Mr. Pugsley's ability. I would ask at the same time why this mad rush to appoint this gentleman with the ability? As far as I can find out from anything he tells us tonight it will be at least years, and it may be decades before* a single dollar will be available for Canada. I do know that the governorship of Ne,w Brunswick became vacant some time ago.
He is out of a job now.
That is a very good reason.
Is there any reason why the vacancy in the Exchequer Court should not be filled, and a judge of that court perform this work?

I have nothing whatever to do -more than assuming my share of responsibility-with the appointment of a judge to the Exchequer Court. I am sure if a judge were appointed he might do the work, but this is not an exchequer court matter at all. It is a matter outside of our courts, a matter of inquiry, being held very frequently outside of this country, to get information upon which this government can reasonably act in reference to a public question such as this.
Are all the hearings held in Ottawa?

Does the hon. member know the legal ability and the great qualifications of the gentleman whom the government have appointed to this position? Evidently the hon. member does not know. I venture to say that if he went to Cape Breton, and from there to Vancouver and British Columbia, traversing the whole of the Do-

Supply-State-War Claims
minion, he would not be able to find a man of greater legal acumen and ability or better qualified to deal with these questions than the Hon. William Pugsley.
I would suggest that they should get the hon. member for Hants (Mr. Martell) to nominate a man for the Exchequer Court, and help them out of their dilemma.

In spite of all my hon. friend's sarcasm, I would suggest that the hon. member for Hants knows many lawyers in Canada quite well qualified to fill the position but the hon. member for Hants undoubtedly, as a supporter of the present administration, having complete faith in them, knows that they will on the right occasion and at the right opportunity, appoint a man with eminent qualifications.
My hon. friend has aspirations himself.

I am sure we are much indebted to the member for Hants for enlightening the House as to the ability of the present commissioner. I really think that the present commissioner has been before the public of Canada long enough for them to judge for themselves of his ability and his particular fitness for the position. I might ask the minister again whether these investigations are all held in Ottawa or whether the commissioner has to travel about the country to hear claims.
He will hold an inquiry whei-ever it is most convenient to hear any number of claims.
How long is it anticipated that this gentleman will be employed at the rate of $9,000 a year and expenses?
I cannot tell my hon. friend.
Is his engagement subject to no definite term?
His services will be dispensed with when he has completed the work he will undertake.
Well, I want to warn the minister that he will be on the job until another one is in sight.

The special pleading of the member for Hants (Mr. Martell) for our old friend Mr. Pugsley, suggests a question to my mind. Upon what basis is th:s eminent legal light to adjudicate these claims? The minister says that the work is not one for which the Exchequer Court is adapted. I gather

from that suggestion that the basis on which the claims will be examined 13 not judicial. Well, is it to be a political basis? H not, I ask again, upon precisely what basis will the claims be adjudicated? The interpolation of my hon. friend for Hants rather arouses in my mind a suspicion that perhaps there is something more than the necessity for eminent legal ability involved in the matter.
To the pure all things are pure.

I will grant that the Hon. Mr. Pugsley possesses great legal ability, but my acquaintance with him in the House also convinces me that few gentlemen in Canada have more political astuteness or adroitness than has that same gentleman. It is natural therefore that we should be very anxious to know exactly the basis upon which these claims are to be adjusted.
Who appointed him governor of New Brunswick?
If the hon. gentleman wants some inside history in regard to that question I can give it to him.
I might agree with you, too.
I have asked the minister a question; I wish he would answer me. Upon what basis are those claims to be adjudicated? The minister declares that it is not to be political. Well, then, what 13 it?

The various claims that are filed will fall into certain categories, and among other things the investigations will be directed towards ascertaining to which of these categories any particular claim belongs. Compensation may be claimed from Germany under article 232 in respect of damage suffered under any one of these categories, of which there are ten. They include:
(1)	Damage to injured persons and to surviving dependants by personal injury to or death of civilians caused by acts of war, including bombardments or other attacks on land, on sea, or from the air, and all the direct consequences thereof, and of all operations of war by the two groups of belligerents whatever arising.
(2)	Damage caused by Germany or her allies to civilian victims of acts of cruelty, violence or maltreatment (including injuries to life or health as a consequence of imprisonment, deportation, internment or evacuation, of exposure at sea or of being forced to labour, wherever arising, and to the surviving dependants of such victims.)
(3)	Damage caused by Germany or her allies in their own territory or in occupied or invaded territory to civilian victims of all acts injurious to health or capacity to work, or to honour, as well as to the surviving dependants of such victims.

Supply-State-War Claims
(4)	Damage caused by any kind of maltreatment of prisoners of war.
(8)	Damage caused to civilians by being forced by Germany or her allies to labour without just remuneration.
(9)	Damage in respect of all property wherever situated belonging to any of the allied or associated states or their nations, with the exception of naval and military works or materials, which has been carried off, seized, injured or destroyed by the acts of Germany or her allies on land, on sea or from the air, or damage directly in consequence of hostilities or of any operations of war.
(10)	Damage in the form of levies, fines and other similar exactions imposed by Germany or her allies upon the civilian population.
These are the various matters in respect of which damages can be claimed and into which investigation will be made.
Does the claimant have to establish legal right?
He has no legal right under the act; it is a mere matter of establishing his claim, and the inquiry is to ascertain whether or not any claim comes within any of the categories 1 have read.

Surely my hon. friend has not the slightest idea of the treaty. It is obvious that whatever rights are given by that solemn covenant are legal rights; the question is entirely a legal one. It is nonsense to say anything else. If therefore this is a matter of legal right why not leave it where it was before? And it is absolutely legal, because the category to which any claim belongs is a matter of legal construction. You might as well say that the rights under a deed or an agreement are not legal. They are legal, just as the rights under a treaty are. My hon. friend says that this is not a proper matter for reference to the Exchequer Court. Why should not the Exchequer . Court have jurisdiction in this matter? There are two possible reasons, and it would be only fair to the minister to let him state his own first if he has any. I would ask him again why cannot this matter be properly looked after by the Exchequer Court?
We no doubt could have a judge of the Exchequer Court act as a commissioner, but I do not think the Exchequer Court would be the proper tribunal.

My recollection is that the Exchequer Court has_ jurisdiction in any matter of this kind; it is a sort of administrative court, and the government has absolute power to refer to it any such question. I should not have thought that there was any doubt about that. But there are, as I say, just two reasons for the action that is intended here. The first is, that
there is a vacancy on the Bench and it is not convenient to the government to appoint the person properly selected for that position during the term of this parliament. That is one reason.
Who is selected?

I think my hon. friend knows very well; if he does not he is not as close to the counsels of his party as I thought he was. But perhaps they are wiser than some people give them credit for being. However that may be, there is another reason. An appointment outside gives the government an excuse for paying so much per annum to a political friend. That is the second reason. There are no other reasons ejxcept those two. Now, my hon. friend says that a commissioner was appointed before-the Chief Justice of New Brunswick. That is true. But my hon. friend will find that that commissioner was to get no 19,000 a year; in fact he was to get nothing at all. Tinder our act he could get nothing except his mere expenses.
Did he do any work?

He did not do
any work. He came up to Ottawa and after the change of administration he gave up the appointment. But for the change of administration the work would have been gone on with just as soon as there was any real necessity for it to be undertaken. Now, the hon. minister knows perfectly well that there are any number of judges quite capable of doing this work -whose services could have been availed of by the administration, but of course in such event there would be no payment of $9,000 a year. Will my hon. friend give me any reasons for this appointment except the two I have advanced?

I can only repeat, Mr'. Chairman, what I have already said. We found it necessary to have a commissioner to investigate this, matter, and as Sir Douglas Hazen, who was appointed a commissioner for this purpose just prior to the going out of office of my hon. friends, afterwards expressed a desire to be relieved of the appointment, we asked Mr. Pugsley to undertake the work. I am sure he will conduct the investigation satisfactorily to the government as well as to parliament.

The hon. gentleman's
answer reminds me of the deaf man who, when called upon to pay a longstanding debt, answered, that it was a very fine day. The question is, why appoint someone who is to be paid a salary when there are any number of members of the Bench whose regular duties
Supply-State-War Claims

are just of this character, determining claims, who could have been appointed. The hon! membei knows quite well that Sir Douglas Hazen upon the accession of this government offered, if it was the will of the government, to place the position at their disposal. Well, of course they eagerly grasped it, and the Honourable William Pugsley now has a large salary at the expense of the state. It is a position demanding legal ability; our judges have legal ability. I do not deny at all that the Hon. William Pugsley has legal ability, but if it is only legal ability that is necessary, it is no news to my hon. friend to be assured that 99 per cent of the talents of the Hon. William Pugsley would be wasted. What I should like to ask is this: after the long list of appointments, east, west, north, south and central, that have gone, with really rather wearisome monotony, to party friends of the government of the deepest dye, ending with the appointment of Mr. Congdon to investigate why the Grand Trunk directors voted gratuities, are many more such appointments still to be made? Is the waiting list long yet? Let us know about when we may expect to get to the end of it.

I am sorry I cannot give my
hon. friend any information.

Have any claims been filed
with the minister's department in regard to what is generally referred to as the Hoppe and Isenberg coal lease?
Nothing has been filed with us.

I hope the suggestion
of the hon. member (Mr. Coote) does not lead the government to appoint another commissioner.

Was this position filled
through- the Civil Service Commission?
I am afraid not.

Why was not this matter
referred to Mr. Justice Audette, the Assistant Judge of the Exchequer Court, and a gentleman very well qualified to deal with claims of this character? There is only one member of the Exchequer Court Bench at the present time. Various names were considered, and it was thought that Mr. Pugsley's name would be the most acceptable to the country generally on account of his ability and experience in that line of work.

The answer to the Secretary of State reveals a rather misty state of mind. He advises the House that one judge is carrying on the business of the Exchequer Court satisfactorily, and that there is no need to appoint another judge.
My hon. friend misunderstood me. I did not say anything like that.

Not in A, B, C, language, but that is the inference which we must take from his observation. But the government finds it necessary to appoint a special commissioner in a judicial capacity to pass upon legal claims, and he says he does not know whether it will be a decade, two decades or three ' decades before this appointment will terminate: he has not the remotest idea. I would suggest to the minister, if he and his colleagues cannot find a suitable appointee for the Exchequer Court vacancy, that the Hon. Mr. Pugsley should be appointed to that court as a judge to carry on this work at the salary of an Exchequer Court judge. He would then have all the machinery of the Exchequer Court at his disposal. My hon. friend and the government are setting up a separate court to do undoubtedly the very thing which the Exchequer Court is supposed to do, and at the same time refraining for a month to appoint a judge to the vacancy in the Exchequer Court. Either the country does not require another judge in the Exchequer Court -in which case why appoint an additional judge?-or else the work of that court does require that another appointment should be made.
I am going to move, Mr. Chairman:
That item No. 382, $75,000 for the Department of the Secretary of State, be reduced by the sum of $9,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The amendment should be put in writing.

I will put it in writing, Mr. Chairman, in a moment.

Supply-State-War Claims

I hardly think my hon. friend can be serious in the amendment that he proposes. We have not increased the expenditure this year; we are not providing for any special outlay. The matter was given very careful consideration, as it was, I am sure prior to the defeat of the government of my hon. friend, when a commissioner was appointed by them to carry out this work. Whether it was because of the change of government I do not know, but Sir Douglas Hazen expressed his desire to be relieved from any duties in that connection. We had hoped that we could get along without appointing another commissioner, but those who had filed claims were pressing very strongly for consideration of those claims by some tribunal, and it was therefore thought advisable that a commissioner should be appointed for the purpose. As to referring the matter to a judge of the Exchequer Court, we have only one judge there at present and we thought it would not be well to ask him to take on this extra work. But aside from that, I doubt whether it would be a proper course to pursue to ask any judge to withdraw his time from his judicial duties in order to attend to an inquiry of this kind. We had a number of names before us for the position. The government of my hon. friend had appointed the Chief Justice of our province, >t man of high standing, and we thought it only right and proper that we should select in his stead a man of ability, of wide legal attainment and experience, a man who for a number of years had occupied the position of Minister of Public Works in the federal government. I am charged with appointing Dr. Pugsley on political grounds, but that same gentleman was so highly thought of, so highly respected by my hon. friends, that he was selected by them to fill the high and honourable position of Lieutenant Governor of the province of New Brunswick.

The minister should do full justice to the subject while he is at it. The late government appointed very many strong Liberals to high positions throughout the entire Dominion. The late government was in no way narrow in that regard.
Nor, were we in any way narrow in appointing the very man whom my hon. friends had appointed as Lieutenant Governor of that province.
We did not make jobs for them, though.

We followed the example of our hon. friends; we selected a man who is admirably qualified to fill the position. My
hon. friend's amendment would only embarrass the department in carrying out its work. If we were asking for a very large increase I could understand my hon. friend taking that position, but under the circumstances I am sure the committee will agree that the amendment should not be accepted.

It is very interesting for the newer members of the House to watch the little battles that take place between the old time parties. It recalls to my mind a certain incident that occurred in the year 1920. A party of twenty-two members of this House went down to St. John, where they were given a dinner, and at the end of the table sat the Hon. Mr. Pugsley, whose name has been mentioned here to-night, and the then Minister of the Interior. As one listened to the complimentary speeches made on that occasion one could not anticipate any such criticism of Mr. Pugsley as we have heard here to-night. On that occasion each handed the other what might be termed bouquets-

Will the hon. gentleman be good enough to substantiate what he says by something in the nature of quotation? I assure him that anything I said I would stand by to-day and am ready to repeat before this House.
The right hon. gentleman sometimes forgets pretty quickly.

Everything was harmonious; if any criticism at all was offered it was directed to one poor timid little Progressive who had only shortly before that reached the House. I know the Minister of the Interior at that time suggested that a new political force-my right hon. friend wants quotation -had arisen in the land, and he predicted that it would be of short duration. The timid little Progressive, responding for Saskatchewan suggested that while everything seemed to run harmoniously between the hon. gentlemen who sat at the head table, representing the two ''old political parties," as they both termed them-"historic political parties"-the day might not be far distant when the new force in the land would relegate the "historic parties" to the prehistoric stage. I say again that as my mind harks back to that occasion- and a very pleasant one it was, I must say -it could not possibly have been anticipated that certain of the gentlemen sitting at that table would subsequently offer any sort oi criticism. The gentleman in question stand-as high in the esteem of the people at the present time as he did then. No crime can be charged against him simply because he
Supply-M ines

happens to be a Liberal, nor could there be if he happened to be a Conservative, and I cannot see why criticism should be levelled against him as it has been. That is the typo of politician I am; I will fight as hard and as honestly for an individual who has politically opposed me at all times as I will for anyone else, provided that he is honest and sincere and capable of filling the position to which he is assigned. That, I think, is a fair expression of the politics that we in this comer of the chamber believe in.

Nobody questions the ability of the Hon. William Pugsley to fill this or any other judicial position, but what hon. gentlemen on this side question is the necessity of the appointment. And we are naturally suspicious when the appointment synchronizes with the completion of his tenure of office as Lieutenant Governor of New Brunswick. It does look to us like a job-
He could not hold both, could he?

No, he could not hold both. He has been known to hold more than one job, but he could not do so in this case- and it is not his fault that he could not. I do submit that the point raised by the hon. member for Centre Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) is well taken and that this commission ership should have been given to one of the judges. Had that been done, there would have been no cost to the country except his necessary expenses.

Another question in regard to oil well inspection. There are several oil wells being drilled in southern British Columbia, and the question arose some short time ago as to whether the companies drilling these wells were dealing with the matter in a fair manner as regards the shareholders and the public. That is, a driller might give out information that there was water in a well and that it was a non-successful operation, and the stock would be sacrificed and gathered in. speechtext: I am going to ask for a small sum in the Supplementary Estimates to pay for the shipment of ore to our testing plant here during this year so that the British Columbia miners may be in fhe same position as those who live very much closer to the Ottawa plant. speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It would be pretty hard to answer that question; we have no knowledge of how much ore will be offered. But I think it will. I think that we

will be able to pay the freight for that amount of money and possibly give tests to ores furnished by all the people in British Columbia who. are interested.

Is the minister aware that there are unlimited quantities of ore in British Columbia awaiting the installation of some ore-testing plant? Does he think that $5,000 or $10,000 would provide that convenience and develop those ore resources?
Mr. STEWART (ArgenteuiU: Of course, my hon. friend knows a great deal more about the subject than I do but the testing of a 200-pound lot will give a fair indication of almost any sample that is forwarded, and $10,000 will bring a great number of lots forward. I am merely suggesting it in order to give some service to the people of British Columbia who have been waiting for some considerable time to have this testing plant established in their province.

I think, perhaps, the minister has not clearly appreciated the point at issue which was referred to by my hon. friend for Kootenay and myself. As a matter of fact there are in British Columbia- and I presume in other sections of the country as well-very large deposits of refractory ores, for instance silver lead and silver zinc ores, with mixtures of other metals that up to the present no commercial plant has been able to profitably separate, although they have been experimenting for years. I was at one, the Trail smelter, one of the finest institutions of the kind in Canada, where they have spent hundreds of thousands of dollars trying to solve this problem. If it were solved it would mean a tremendous saving to the country and an impetus to the mining business generally, not only in British Columbia but wherever such ores are found Now, the expenditure contemplated in the location of an ore testing plant-at least the amount set a few years ago-was in the neighbourhood of $100,000. It was recognized then that the establishment of such a plant would cost probably from $100,000 to S200,-000. There was a difficulty in the minds of the officials of the department as to the best place to locate that plant, whether in the interior or on the coast. Personally I have never expressed any opinion-I do not think I am competent to do so-as to where it should be located. The officials of the department should determine that in the interest of the investigatory work; it is very important. I want to say to the minister that I appreciate this contemplated vote of $10,000 to test these small samples of ores, but that 
will not do very much good m solving the problem I mention. It must be treated on a commercial basis, and it will perhaps take some years to find a process that will successfully treat these ores. I am certain that the return would amply repay the department for the investigation. I am very sorry if the former vote has been dropped from the estimates, because what the minister now suggests to replace it will not meet the case at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have given the matter some consideration and I do not think $50,000 would construct the plant that would be required in British Columbia.
What amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I should say $100,000, I do not know whether double the amount, which would involve an annual expenditure of some $50,000. would do. In the meantime I thought it wise to offer facilities to the British Columbia miner who is desirous of having tests made of the product of his particular mine or claim. If he agrees to forward samples here from his nearest railway station we will give him all the tests that he would probably get at the inception of a plant in his own province. Of course I quite follow my hon. friend's suggestion that this plant would require developments as various ores came to it for the purpose of determining a proper course of treating, but we do identically the same testing work here. I am quite of the opinion that a plant of this character will have to be established in British Columbia but I may say, generally speaking, that unless there is an absolute dire necessity for the building of this plant ou,t there and the purchase of the necessary machinery I think it well to delay matters, at least for a year, in the hope that both machinery and building costs will be reduced. However, I have no desire to penalize the very important industry in British Columbia, and in the meantime this required service will be given for the benefit of the province.

In view of the fact that a vote wns passed some time ago and has been allowed to lapse, representing a district that depends entirely upon its mineral resources. I give it as my opinion, and the opinion of those better able to speak with authority than I am, that such action is penalizing the people of British Columbia and especially the mining industry. At the present time that industry in British Columbia is on the eve of improvement. There never was a time in the last eight years when the

Supply-Mines
outlook was as good as it now is. We have this smelter situated at Trail, the property of the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company, a very large institution doing a great deal of work for the province. Nevertheless, there are many kinds of complex ores throughout the province, and in the districts where they have these ores they require a testing plant. The minister has mentioned this small plant located at Nelson. As I am particularly conversant with this plant, and as I know how it happened that it is situated there I can tell the minister that, with a small expenditure, it would be in a position to handle the process of testing these different complex ores in the initial stages. This plant can be made available with a very smjill expenditure. By holding up this vote which was put through in the last few years, I think the government is holding back the mining industry and the assistance that it should have in developing what is considered our greatest asset.

I am fully in sympathy with this move to get a plant out in British Columbia to test ore, but I think the government should investigate the situation in order to ascertain the most feasible place to locate the plant. Personally, I think Kamloops is about the most central location, and I would ask the government to go fully into the question, in order to ascertain the most feasible place to put the plant so as to give accommodation to everybody. We have both the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific railways at Kamloops. It is well supplied with railways.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In reply to both hon. members, I may say that I am entirely in sympathy with the idea of establishing a plant. I believe the mining industry warrants the placing of a plant in British Columbia. There is the practical difficulty raised by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride). We have made some investigation of the plant the hon. member for Kootenay (Mr. Humphrey) speaks of. We have not approached the owners for the purpose of finding out what it could be purchased for. It occurred to me that probably that plant was not favourably located to serve the needs of British Columbia, and that would need some investigation as well. It would serve the needs of southern British Columbia entirely, but as mining is carried on, and probably will be carried on, throughout the whole British Columbia region when the plant is built, I think it should be placed as near a central point as possible, in order
that freight costs may be reduced to a minimum. What we will do this year I think will give the service to every man very reasonably. If a man brings his samples to the station, puts them on the train
10 p.m. and sends them forward we will agree to give them a test and return him the results of the test. I do not want it to be inferred that, because we have not put an amount in the estimates for the construction of the plant this year, the idea has been dropped, because it has not.

Is it the intention of the department to carry on further investigations in regard to establishing this plant in British Columbia this year, or is this the final move, providing an appropriation for bringing the ore to Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No. 1
thought I made it clear to my hon. friend that this was only a temporary measure to cover the year. We will certainly try to place the plant where it will be most convenient. The question of whether it is wise to establish a plant has been settled so far as I can ascertain from the officials of the department. There are no two opinions about that, but there is some question as to whether it should go right down to the coast where the railways all concentrate, or whether it should be put in a central portion of the province, as suggested by my hon. friend for Kamloops, or some place where cross-country railways would serve the interests of all parties concerned.

The department could very well decide the location of the plant, if they would admit the principle of establishing one in British Columbia. This question has been considered and certainly negotiations have been carried on for a number of years back. The mining people of British Columbia feel that they are being penalized by the government not being able to reach a decision. Representations are being made to the department in respect to particular points, and the desire is to co-operate, and to render any assistance that may be possible to the department to assist them to come to a decision. It is not for the particular benefit of one point or one locality so much as to render some assistance and co-operation to enable the government to come to a decision. Representing a district that is entirely a mining district, I could not do otherwise than bring out the qualifications of that particular district, especially in regard to the plant now located at Nelson. That plant

could be acquired practically without any outlay of money. A very small sum would purchase it, and it is equipped with something like 840,000 or $50,000 worth of machinery which is lying idle. I simply offer these suggestions with a view to assisting the government. This particular point is located in the interior, where there is practically the greatest amount of complex ore, and it is easily accessible from any other point in the province.
Is it the intention of the government to give any assistance to the Coast Range Steel Company? I believe that company has asked for a guarantee of bonds, or something of that' kind.

speechtext: Representations have been made to the government but, so far as I know, no commitments of any kind have been made.

What success has the
department had in drilling for oil in southern Alberta? When I was there last fall, at what is known as the Maclean well, they had reached a depth of about 1,900 feet. speechtext: I understood my hon. friend to say that the department was drilling. The department does not do any drilling, but I can give my hon. friend some information about the Coutts Sweet Grass Company. They have reached a depth now of 2,800 feet, and we know that in all cases of drilling for oil you may be 50 feet off the basin in which the oil is located and miss it. They, like other drillers, are very confident that they will get oil, but whether they will or not I cannot say. They make the statement that at 2,200 feet they struck a small vein but did not think it of sufficient volume to warrant the stopping of drilling operations, and so they went to a greater depth.
I understand that they are going further.

speechtext: For geological survey, the item under discussion, we estimate for exploration in British Columbia and Yukon, which are combined in the item, $38,300; in the Northwest territories, $5,000; in Alberta, $17,000; in Manitoba, $4,500; in Saskatchewan, $4,500; in Ontario, $24,200; in Quebec, $11,000; in New Brunswick, $3,000; in Nova Scotia, $6,500; and "in general," $2,300. In connection with the topographical surveys we will spend in British Columbia, $12,000; in Manitoba, $4,500; in Ontario, $8,500; in Quebec $8,600; in New Brunswick. $6,000, and in Nova Scotia $8,000. A question was raised last year by the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), and I think by the member for Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), in regard to an apparent over-lapping, and the matter was looked into. At first I had an idea that it would perhaps be well to combine all topographical surveys under the Surveys branch, but I find that some years ago the Geological branch were desirous of controlling the work for the purpose of mapping areas upon which geological work was to be carried on; and they did that work under their direction. I find also that in the Department of National Defence some work was being carried on. Under the chairmanship of Doctor Deville we have taken care to see that there is no overlapping in the work, and hence you will find a variation in the expenditures in the Geological branch and the Topographical branch in the various provinces. I can assure the committee-and this is the point I wish to make-that there is absolutely no overlapping; the operations carried on by the various organizations, are co-ordinated and made use of. For example, if in any section the geological parties have already done the topographical work, then there is no party from the Topographical branch doing work there.

I do not think that the minister had any task in stopping overlapping. I had a survey committee at work for some time while I was in the department some years ago, and under the chairmanship of Doctor Deville I provided successfully against overlapping. What I called attention to a year ago was something in regard to which apparently I was not able to influence the government-that is, the survey

work being done in the Militia department. If any human being can tell me of what value that is to this country, then the information would be in addition to my knowledge.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They have joined us on the board; we do not know what they are doing.
Did my hon. friend say that they are joined under the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No; they work with us; we know what they are doing.
I know what they are doing too, and it is because I know what they are doing that I think the work is worthless; and it is very expensive.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The topographical work?

Yes. They are doing such thorough topographical survey work that in the area they have covered you can tell where every schoolhouse is, where every church is, where every house is, almost where every telegraph pole is, if not the height of it. It is really a sort of literal photograph of the entire country; and they have done now so much after about twenty-five years of work that if -they can keep on through next millennium and half of the following one, they will have done. Such is the nature of their work; and by the time they are about one-hundredth part through, the beginning of the work will be of no use, because all these things change. I do hope that the minister will exert his influence to see that worthless survey work is done away with. I do not find fault with the officers; I think they are doing their work well. But of what value the work is to -the country for the amount of money expended I never was able to understand. I sincerely trust that now that the attention of the government is called .to the matter this work will be done away with. I did not know about it until close to the termination of my office. May I suggest another thing to the minister for the exercise of his dormant talents, if he has any left after the Interior department is taken care of. He should try to avoid unnecessary expenditure and save some money for serving the country. There is a necessity in connection with that ore-dressing plant in British Columbia. I remember being entirely convinced of an urgent necessity there. I cannot say that I can bring the reasons to bear just now why it is not possible, effectively and with practical results, to bring ore here. What the
minister has in mind may possibly alleviate the situation for a while, but he will find that in the end jt will likely have been better for him to have saved the money and got sooner to work constructing a proper ore-dressing plant. So convinced was I of this that in the last year I was in office an estimate was put in for the purpose of starting work in this direction. But of course the contest came on that year and we could not go on. Let the minister exert his energy to prevent the appointment of grotesque commissions, and the prolific creation of fancy sinecures for party friends, and then there will be some money left for work of this kind that goes to develop wealth in the country. The minister has an ore-dressing plant in one part of the city of Ottawa; I forget the street. The plant is a good one and it is not expensive and it is to that plant that this ore will come. Some two or three years ago we were testing there new methods of ore flotation. It is well known that the mineral flotation people have a patent method of flotation by oil which they control and out of which they exact very large profits, making the company immensely wealthy. A new flotation system was being tried and, before I left, had met with very encouraging success. I should like to know whether that success has been continued, and what the opinion of the department is as to its value.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: One of the difficulties in connection with research work of this character is to convince parliament and the people that the money is well expended. We have made a very heavy expenditure at Bienfait on experimental work with fuel which has not yet resulted successfully The experiments mentioned by my hon. friend are still going on, and I watched them with a good deal of interest last year in the plant there. We are asking for some money to buy improved machinery. I had the deputy minister visit England, Germany, and Belgium as well as keep very closely in touch with the Bureau of Mines of the American government in order that we may know what other people are accomplishing in research work respecting new methods of treating ores as well as fuels and so get value for the money we expend and perhaps discover better methods of handling these problems. No very great success however, has yet attended the experimental work that my hon. friend has referred to.
The liquid flotation?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Nothing
that we can say is a definite success.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot give that information at the moment. I saw them experimenting there, but not on lead.
On gold?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
It was considered rather successful on gold in my time. Has that opinion been reversed?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am told on copper and gold they have got definite success.
Has this department any revenue from some of the provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
Does not the government control the mineral rights in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Have you not revenue from mining and oil leases?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, but
that is in the Interior department; this is the Mines department, which is entirely separate.
You have no revenue from British Columbia or the other provinces in this connection?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not in this department.
We could get particulars of the revenue when the estimates of the Interior are brought down?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Revenue from what?

Revenue from leases of mineral and oil rights. It seems to me it is a question that should be looked into as to just how much money we should spend on provinces that have their own mineral resources when there are other provinces that have been deprived of such resources, and I do not know whether any money has been spent to help the latter develop these resources.

I can tell my hon. friend that money has been spent, and the fact that those provinces were deprived of their resources has been a consideration in spending more money there. There is a very, very large expenditure in geological survey work in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta, par-

ticularly in the northern parts of those provinces where our chief finds were. Of course, in British Columbia there has been the greatest expenditure because British Columbia is really by nature where the best results could be expected.

It may be true that British Columbia has the greatest mineral resources, and those resources will enure to the benefit of British Columbia alone in that sense. So that the prairie provinces are not being justly dealt with in this regard. I would point out the injustice that Alberta is suffering from at the present time. We have on our statute books an act governing the payment of bounty on crude oil according to its specific gravity, and the standard is set in such a peculiar way that I think none of the wells in Alberta have been able to secure any bounty, although the Dominion owns those resources and has received large amounts in rentals from oil leases; but the government is paying considerable sums every year for crude oil produced in Ontario, and there the provincial authorities own the mineral rights. I think it is time the government amended the act so that crude oil produced in Alberta may be given the same bounty as the Ontario crude oil. For the last eleven years the Alberta oil men have been trying to get successive governments to change the act, but so far without success. Before this session closes I hope the government will see that this injustice to Alberta is removed. It is certainly aggravating when one considers that the Dominion owns the oil resources in Alberta and yet refuses to give a bounty to the crude oil that is being produced there, although the oil producers in Ontario are given this advantage notwithstanding the fact that the oil rights there, as I said before, are owned by the provincial government.

As the payment of these
bounties is under my department. I may sa}r that the act in question was passed long before oil was discovered in Alberta, and that its provisions do not discriminate in any way against Alberta or any of the other western provinces. The same specific gravity applies to Alberta as to Ontario oil, but apparently only the latter oil comes within the act. However, the observations made by my hon. friend have the consideration of the government, and it is quite possible that we may amend the act, if not this session then next session.

I am quite pleased to hear that this matter has the consideration of the government but I believe it has had the

consideration of successive governments for quite a number of years. The trouble is that the government of the day never does anything but consider this matter. I want to serve warning on this government right here and now that if more than one session elapses after this session, and the act is not amended, there is going to be war right in this House on this particular matter.
Who is going to make it?

If nobody else will I will
make it myself.
It seems to me this is the same old story; the state will bonus private individuals, but when it comes to bonusing its own industry it refuses to do so.
It is not our own.

In Ontario it is not a much more difficult task to drill an oil well than it is to drill a water well, but in going after oil in Alberta they drill on an average from 3,000 to 5,000 feet, and that is an expensive operation. It is very hard to get oil prospectors to risk enough money to put down an oil well, some of which cost in the neighbourhood of $100,000. So far as this bounty is concerned, if the government will cease paying it to Ontario I will be quite satisfied. 1 want these oil men put on an equal basis; 1 think we have good ground for demanding that. I do not want to discuss the question further at present, because I am not armed with the statistics I would like to have.
Would my hon. friend be really willing to have that done?
I am quite willing to have it done.

Then the government would simply have to act as the private individual does in Ontario-make the oil man pay rent right from the start, give him no credit at all on his capital investment, then when he gets the product charge him a royalty on it. I assure my hon. friend it would be no hardship on the country to allow the exploiter, under those conditions, a bonus under the Bounty Act.

I do not see why the government would be compelled to do any such thing. If they simply cease to pay the oil. bounty in Ontario that need not entail the dire results that the right hon. gentleman suggests..
That is exactly equal treatment.

I do not want to get away from the item that is being considered.

Control of the composition and method of manufacture of explosives disclosed by manufacturers confidentially, and examined for authorization for manufacture and storage in Canada or for importation.
